The language of the first inhabitants of this island, beyond doubt, was the Celtic, or Gaelic, common to them with Gaul; liom which country, appears, by many it circumstances, that Great Britain was peopled. þÿ This Celtic tongue, which is said to be very expressive and copious, and is, probably, one of the most ancient languages in the world, prevailed once in most of the western regions of Europe, It was the language of Gaul, of Gteat Britain, of Ireland, and, veiy probably, of Spain also : till, in the course of those revolutions, which, by means of the conquests, hist of the Romans, and afterwards of the northern nations, changed the government, speech, and, in a manner, the whole face of Europe, this language was gradually obliterated, and now subsits only in the mountains of Wales, in the Highlands of Scotland, and m Ireland : for the Welsh, the Erse, and the Irish, are no other than dtllerent dialects of the same tongue, the ancient Celtic. This, then, was the language of the primitive Britons, the fust inhabitants, that we know of, in our island; and continued so till the arrival of the Saxons in England, in the \ ear of our Lord 450; they, having conquered the Britons, did not intermix with them, but expelled them from their habitations, and drove them, together with their language,

into the mountains of Wales. The Saxons wise one of those northern nations that overrun Europe; and their tongue, a dialect of the Gothic, or Teutonic, altogether distinct trim the Celtic, laid the foundation of the present English tongue. With some intermixture of Danish, (a language, probably, Iron) the same root with the Snxon), it con tinued to tie spoken throughout the southern part of the island, till the lime ol W illiam the Conqueror. The history of the English language can, in this manner, be clearly traced, lhe language spoken in the low countries ol Scotland, is now, and has been for many centuries, no other than a dialect of i ho English. HAMBURG, JUNK 1. Nothing particular interest has occurred of for the last three or four days in Schleswig- Holstein and Fiilmen. The operations both of the Germans and Danes have been at a stand still, in expectation, it would appear, of instructions from Berlin. Nothing has yet transpired of the result of the negotiations between the Prussian Cabinet and Chamberlain lieediz The dates from Jutland are Aarhuus the 28th, Fredericia the 29th ult. The Danish General Rye still kept his position a few miles north of Aarhuus, whereas General i'rittwitz, with his forces, remained a few miles south of the town, on the border of the sea. Near Fredericia a few shots had been exchanged on the 28th be tween the Sohleswig-Holstein batteries and the Danish batteries on Fuhnen. The Schleswig-Holsteiners were erecting more batteries close to the walls of Frederi cia. For the rest all was quiet. Last night the Danes again appeared near the entrance of the Bay of Kiel with their line of battleship. a frigate, and a steamer of war. A few shots were fired from the batteries towards the frigate approaching nearest, when the stops made of) again. Orla Lehmanti, the famous Danish agitator, is still kept prisoner, and from the town of Schleswig, where he was allowed to walk about for his recreation, against his word of honour not to escape, it was louod proper to remove him to the fortress of Kendsburg as a safer abode. The Danish blockading squadron in the N'"lbSea was recently strengthened by the

artival of the war steamer Geyser. APPEAL is made to the members of the English Congregation and others for Subscriptions to the fund for the restoration and extension of the Parish Church of St John's. Its neglected state and the Insufficiency of its sittings for the accommodation of the Congregation seem imperatively to demand this work. V it h a population of 4500 members, with over 1000 Communicants, with an average daily attendance on its live Sunday Schools of 800 þÿ the Church contains sittings for only 400, exclusive of the Aisles and Gallery, and when these are crowded as at present, only 1000. Most oflhe pupils of the Sunday School and many communicants, arc, for want of accommodations, excluded from the public serv ices of the sanctuary. To meet this want the Rector and Vestry ask the co-operation of the Planters, Merchants and others, believing that they will recognize with them, the manifest duty, both ill a civil and religions view, of assisting to provide additional sittings for the poor labouring population, who, we arc happy to make known, have very generally subscribed to a weekly stiver subscription in aid of this object, the subscriptions of which already amount to $ 2,700 for the year. May the GOD of all grace give his people willing hearts that we make not the rebuke of the Projdiet our own. Subscription lists are in circulation. St. Giioix June Hth 1849.

CROIX, Christians ted, Monday, June 11th 1819. ON last Saturday the 9th Inst, the first Stone of the new Catholic Church in Christiansted, to be dedicated to the Virgin and Holy Cross was laid bv His Excellency Governor General P. Hansen. After High Mass was sung by the Reverend T. E Butler, and a brief explanation given of the ceremony, þÿ the procession then moved on from the temporary Chapel, to the spot destined to receive the foundation Stone. After the litanies &c. were chanted, the Revd. Butler, in the absence ot the Bishop sprinkled the first Slone and the foundation with Holy Water. A Silver trowel was then presented to His Excellency who laid the mortar, and the first stone was let down into its birth. A second stone was afterwards laid by C. Mac Evoy Esq , as the representative ot the Congregation. The foundations were again sprinkled with Holy Water and the ceremony concluded. In a hollow of the Stone, a small ornamented Box was placed, containing a scroll of paper, and several coins of different dates; the paper bore the following inscription : þÿ The first stone of the new Church under the patronage of the Virgin and Holy Cross was laid by His Excellency Governor General P- Hansen on the 9th of June 1849; our Most Holy Father Pope Pius the 9th, reigning ; the Right Reverend Doctor Smith, being Vicar Apostolic of the Danish Westindia Islands, and the Reverend Tus. E. Butler, Pastor of the þÿplace. After the ceremony was concluded. His Excellency and several gentlemen partook of lunch at the Presbytery.

Dresden wa3 the scene of a sanguinary contest on the 3d and 4th instant, the people having risen in consequence of the despotic conduct of the King of Saxony. The civic guard took part with the people, who succeeded in repulsing the military at several points, and gained entire possession of the Old Town, The city was studded with barricades. On the 5th, 2000 Prussian troops arrived, and imirediately occupied a portion ol the Old Town. On the 0th instant the ancient Opeia House was in flames, and it Was feared that the Prince's Palace would not escape destruction On the 7th, the conflict was resumed. On the 8lh inst , hostilities still raged between the Koyalists and the insurgents, to the dis advantage of the latter, without any imme diate prospect of their termination. The inembets of the Provisional Government had been outlawed, and rewards offered for their apprehension. At Leipsic, also, disturbances had broken out, but after a short and sharp struggle be tween the military aud the populace they were suppressed. .Several of the rioters were killed.

A short time before tits arrival, some naval officers, belonging to an Austrian frigate, which had put into the prut of Caifla, came to the monastery, which is situated on the mountain, and which aflords hospitality to strangers. þÿ Their visit being ended, tin v requested a voting lad, who acted as a kind ol domestic in the convent, to show them a shot l way down the mountain, to their long-boat. lie complied, and. after accompanying them n considerable distance, was returning tranquilly to the house of the Cotnmui it y , when, on a sudden, lie beheld an enormous panther rushing down upon him. At the sight of this formidable animal, alone as he was, and without strength to use arms, even if he was provided with them, his sensations may he easily imagined His knees bent under him, and he fell himself absolutely incapable of advancing or tecediug a single step. Meanwhile. in the twinkling ol an eye the panther reached him. Sporting with its prey, in the manner of a cat with a tiioUsu Which she lias taken, the ferocious animal began to take different positions, Varying its attitudes, alid seeking to touch him with its foot, as if to tantalise him ; then removing suddenly to the

dist nice of some paces, darted rapidly upon him The poor youth understood Very well by what he had heard of the unhappy fate of othets in a similar case, in wliat manner this frightful sport was to terminate ; he believed that his Inst hour was come. In this frightful position, destitute of all human succour, he <1td not, however, loiget the lessons of his Christian education, which taught him, that in every extremity man fms no invisible friend, the Lord and Maker of men and animals, whose eats ate ever open to the cry of the distressed, and who, if he sees it expedient for n» can «i any time rescue ns from danger.
